prompt: What is the unit of electric current? (Give the name or the symbol.)
hints: It's measured with an **am**meter.
solution: Current is measured in **amps (A)**, using an ammeter.

prompt: What do we call a material that lets electric current flow through it easily?
hints: Copper wire is a good example.
solution: A **conductor**. Metals such as copper are good conductors. Materials that don't let current flow, like plastic, are **insulators**.

prompt: Match each item to the correct description.
hints: The names of the meters give you a clue: AMmeter → AMps, VOLTmeter → VOLTs.
solution: Current → amps; voltage → volts; resistance → ohms; ammeter → measures current; voltmeter → measures voltage.

prompt: Two objects both have a negative charge. What happens when they are brought close together?

options.text: They repel (push apart)
They attract (pull together)
Nothing happens
They both become positive

feedback.b: Opposite (unlike) charges attract. These two charges are the same.
feedback.c: Charged objects always push or pull on each other.
feedback.d: Bringing them close together doesn't change their charge.

hints: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
solution: They have **like** (the same) charges, so they **repel**.

prompt: Select **all** the materials that are good electrical **conductors**.

prompt: Ella rubs a balloon on her hair. The balloon becomes **negatively** charged. Why?

options.text: Electrons moved from her hair onto the balloon
Positive charges moved from the balloon onto her hair
Rubbing created new negative charges on the balloon
Electrons moved from the balloon onto her hair

feedback.b: Positive charges don't move when you rub materials. Only electrons do.
feedback.c: Charge can't be created. It moves from one object to another.
feedback.d: If the balloon lost electrons, it would become positive.

hints: Only electrons (negative charges) can move when you rub two materials together.
solution: Electrons (negative) moved from the hair **onto** the balloon. The balloon gained electrons, so it's negative; her hair lost electrons, so it's positive.

options.text: It goes out, because the circuit is now broken
It stays on at the same brightness
It gets brighter, because it gets all the current
It flickers on and off

feedback.b: That happens in a parallel circuit, where each lamp has its own branch.
feedback.c: With the loop broken, no current flows at all.
feedback.d: Once the loop is broken, no current flows, so the lamp stays off.

hints: A series circuit has only one path for the current.
solution: In a series circuit there's only **one path**. A blown lamp breaks the loop, so no current flows and the other lamp **goes out**.

prompt: Two balloons are both rubbed on a wool jersey and then hung on threads next to each other. What happens?

options.text: They push apart, because they have the same type of charge
They pull together, because they have opposite charges
Nothing, because balloons are insulators
They pull together, because all charged objects attract

feedback.b: Both balloons were charged the same way, so their charges are the same, not opposite.
feedback.c: Insulators can hold static charge. That's why static builds up on them.
feedback.d: Like charges repel. Only unlike charges attract.

hints: Both balloons were rubbed with the same material in the same way.
solution: Both balloons gain the **same** type of charge, and **like charges repel**, so they push apart.

prompt: Explain why a balloon that has been rubbed on your hair is then attracted to your hair.
modelAnswer: When the balloon is rubbed on the hair, electrons (negative charges) move from the hair onto the balloon. The balloon gains electrons, so it becomes negatively charged. The hair loses electrons, so it becomes positively charged. Unlike (opposite) charges attract, so the balloon and hair pull towards each other.

rubric.criterion: Electrons move from the hair to the balloon when they are rubbed
The balloon becomes negative and the hair becomes positive
Opposite (unlike) charges attract

hints: Which particles move when two materials are rubbed together?
What charge does each object end up with?
solution: Rubbing moves **electrons** from the hair to the balloon. Balloon: negative. Hair: positive. **Unlike charges attract.**

prompt: A third lamp is added in **series** to a circuit with two lamps. The total resistance [[a]], so the current [[b]], and all the lamps get [[c]].
hints: Each lamp resists the current. What happens when there are more of them in one loop?
solution: More lamps in series means more **resistance**, so the **current decreases** and every lamp gets **dimmer**. The battery's voltage is also shared between more lamps.

prompt: Two lamps are connected in **parallel** to a battery. Lamp L1 is unscrewed. What happens to lamp L2?

options.text: It stays on, at about the same brightness
It goes out
It gets much brighter, because it now gets all the voltage
It gets dimmer

feedback.b: That happens in series. In parallel, L2 has its own complete path.
feedback.c: L2 already had the full battery voltage across it, so it doesn't change.
feedback.d: L2's branch still has the full voltage across it.

hints: Does L2's branch still make a complete loop with the battery?
solution: L2 is on its own branch, which still makes a complete loop with the battery, and it still has the full battery voltage. It **stays on at the same brightness**.

prompt: Compare **series** and **parallel** circuits. In your answer, describe the paths for the current, what happens to the current and the voltage, and what happens if one lamp breaks.
modelAnswer: A series circuit has only one path (one loop), while a parallel circuit has two or more separate branches. In series, the current is the same everywhere in the circuit; in parallel, the current splits at the junctions and the branch currents add up to the total. In series, the battery voltage is shared between the components; in parallel, each branch gets the full battery voltage. If one lamp breaks in a series circuit, the loop is broken and all the lamps go out; in a parallel circuit, the other branches still work.

rubric.criterion: Paths: series has one loop; parallel has separate branches
Current: the same everywhere in series; splits and adds up in parallel
Voltage: shared between components in series; full voltage across each branch in parallel
Broken lamp: all go out in series; the others stay on in parallel

The wall is always positively charged
The balloon's electrons flow into the wall and glue it in place
Air pressure pushes the balloon against the wall

feedback.b: The wall is neutral overall: it has equal amounts of positive and negative charge.
feedback.c: The wall is an insulator, so charge doesn't flow into it easily, and charge isn't a glue.

The lamps in circuit X (series)

In each circuit, the lamp nearest the battery is brightest

feedback.b: In series the lamps share the battery voltage, so each gets less.
feedback.c: Series lamps share the voltage, but parallel lamps each get the full voltage.
feedback.d: Current isn't used up along a wire, so position doesn't matter.

hints: Compare the voltage across each lamp in the two circuits.
solution: In series, the two lamps **share** the battery voltage (half each). In parallel, **each** lamp gets the **full** battery voltage, so more current flows through each one and the parallel lamps are **brighter**.

prompt: Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity. Explain how lightning happens, using ideas about electric charge.
modelAnswer: Inside a storm cloud, ice crystals and water droplets are thrown around and rub or collide with each other. This moves charge between them, so the cloud becomes charged: usually the bottom of the cloud is negative. A huge amount of charge builds up, and the large difference in charge between the cloud and the ground (opposite charges attract) becomes so great that the charge suddenly jumps through the air as a giant spark. This sudden flow of charge, a discharge, is lightning.

rubric.criterion: Collisions/rubbing between ice and water particles in the cloud move charge, so charge builds up (e.g. the bottom of the cloud is negative)
There is a large difference in charge between the cloud and the ground; opposite charges attract
When the charge is big enough it suddenly flows through the air as a giant spark (discharge)

hints: Static charge builds up when things rub together. What is rubbing together inside a storm cloud?

solution: Rubbing and colliding ice and water particles charge the cloud. A large charge builds up, opposite to the ground. When it's big enough, the charge suddenly jumps through the air (a **discharge**), and that spark is lightning.

prompt: Some strings of party lights (fairy lights) are wired in parallel, like the lamps in this circuit. Explain why wiring the lights in parallel is more convenient than wiring them all in series.
modelAnswer: In parallel, each lamp is on its own branch, so if one lamp breaks or is taken out, the others still have a complete path and stay on. In series, one broken lamp breaks the whole loop and every lamp goes out. Also, each lamp in parallel gets the full voltage, so the lights stay bright even when there are lots of them. In series the voltage would be shared, so every extra lamp would make them all dimmer.

rubric.criterion: If one lamp breaks, the others stay on in parallel (each has its own path), but in series they would all go out
Each lamp gets the full voltage in parallel, so they stay bright; in series the voltage is shared, so they would be dimmer

hints: What happens in each type of circuit if one lamp blows?
How is the voltage shared in each type of circuit?
solution: Parallel wiring keeps the other lamps working if one fails, and gives every lamp the full voltage.

feedback.c: The electrons the comb gained came from the jersey, so the jersey is left with fewer electrons than protons.
feedback.d: Protons don't move when things are rubbed together. Only electrons move.

hints: Where did the comb's extra electrons come from?
solution: Electrons moved **from the jersey onto the comb**. The comb now has extra electrons (negative), and the jersey has fewer electrons than protons, so it is **positively** charged.

prompt: After walking across the classroom carpet in his socks, Tama touches a metal door handle and feels a small electric shock. Explain why this happens.
modelAnswer: As Tama walks, his socks rub on the carpet and electrons are transferred, so static charge builds up on his body. The metal door handle is a good conductor. When his hand gets close to it, the built-up charge suddenly flows between his hand and the handle, sometimes as a tiny spark. This sudden flow of charge (a discharge) is the shock he feels.

rubric.criterion: Rubbing on the carpet transfers electrons, so static charge builds up on his body
The metal handle is a conductor, so charge can flow through it easily
The charge suddenly flows (jumps) between his hand and the handle as a spark or discharge, which he feels as a shock

hints: What happens when two materials rub together?
Why does it happen with a metal handle, but not with a wooden door?
solution: Rubbing builds up static charge; touching a conductor lets it all flow away suddenly, which is the shock.

A battery, even if there is a gap in the wires

prompt: Describe how you would connect an ammeter and a voltmeter to measure the current through a lamp and the voltage across it. Include the units each meter measures in.
modelAnswer: The ammeter is connected in series with the lamp, in the same loop, so the current that flows through the lamp also flows through the ammeter. It measures current in amps (A). The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the lamp, with one wire joined on each side of the lamp. It measures voltage in volts (V).

rubric.criterion: Ammeter connected in series with the lamp (in the same loop)
Voltmeter connected in parallel across the lamp (one wire on each side of it)
Correct units: current in amps (A) and voltage in volts (V)

hints: One meter goes in the loop, and one goes across the lamp. Which is which?
solution: Ammeter: in series, measures amps (A). Voltmeter: in parallel across the component, measures volts (V).

prompt: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a battery, and they are quite dim. Using the same battery and lamps, how could Mia make both lamps brighter?

Add a third identical lamp in series
Swap the two lamps around
Move the lamps closer to the battery

feedback.b: A third lamp in series shares the voltage even more and adds resistance, so all the lamps would get **dimmer**.
feedback.c: In series the same current flows through both lamps, so swapping them changes nothing.
feedback.d: Moving lamps along a wire doesn't change the current or the voltage they get.

hints: In which type of circuit does each lamp get the whole battery voltage?
solution: In series the lamps share the battery voltage. In **parallel**, each lamp gets the **full** voltage, so a bigger current flows through each lamp and both are brighter. (The battery will go flat faster, though.)

prompt: When fuel is pumped quickly through a hose into a fuel tanker or a plane, static charge can build up. Explain why the vehicle is connected to the ground with a metal wire before the fuel starts to flow.
modelAnswer: As the fuel rubs against the inside of the hose, electrons are transferred, so static charge can build up on the hose and the vehicle. If enough charge builds up, it could jump as a spark, and a spark could set fire to the fuel vapour and cause a fire or an explosion. The metal wire is a conductor, so the charge flows safely along it into the ground as soon as it forms, instead of building up enough to make a spark.

rubric.criterion: Friction (rubbing) between the fuel and the hose transfers electrons, so static charge builds up
A build-up of charge could cause a spark, which could set fire to the fuel vapour (fire or explosion)
The metal wire is a conductor, so the charge flows safely to the ground (earthing) instead of building up

hints: What happens when two materials rub against each other?
Why is a spark especially dangerous near fuel?
solution: Earthing gives the static charge a safe path to the ground, so it never builds up enough to make a spark near flammable fuel.

prompt: Three identical lamps are connected in parallel to a battery. The ammeter in the main wire reads 0.9 A. One lamp is unscrewed. What does the main ammeter read now?
hints: Identical lamps in parallel each carry the same share of the total current.
Unscrewing one lamp doesn't change the current in the other branches.
solution: Each branch carries $0.9 \div 3 = 0.3$ A. Unscrewing one lamp breaks only that branch; the other two still carry 0.3 A each. New total $= 0.3 + 0.3 =$ **0.6 A**.
